We think of a final “blocked” configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks, each lying in one row or one column, so that no further such block remains. Call any three consecutive positions in a row or column a “potential triple.” Each row contains \(\max\{n-2,0\}\) horizontal potential triples, and each column contains the same number of vertical potential triples. Hence
\[
H=V=n\max\{n-2,0\},\qquad T=2n\max\{n-2,0\}.
\]
In particular, these counts are zero when \(n=1\), and for \(n\ge2\) they equal \(H=V=n(n-2)\) and \(T=2n(n-2)\). Since the configuration is blocked, every potential triple must be hit, meaning that at least one of its stamps has been removed.","claim":"Defines potential triples, correctly counts them for every positive integer n, including n=1, and states that every potential triple is hit in a blocked configuration.","depends_on":[],"scope":[],"goal_refs":[]}],"target_dependencies_after":[],"counterexample":null,"reason":"Replacing n(n−2) by n max{n−2,0} fixes the negative count at n=1 while preserving the original count for n≥2 and leaving the hitting argument unchanged."}

(I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
